Volume 10 · Chapter 08

Black-Scholes and risk-neutral valuation

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v10-c07

By the endDerive the pricing equation and distinguish a model's assumptions from market conventions.

Capability, prerequisites and the pricing question

After this chapter you should be able to derive the dividend-adjusted Black–Scholes equation from a funded trading strategy, construct its pricing probability measure, integrate the terminal payoff to obtain European call and put prices, and identify exactly where the result stops applying. The prerequisite is Brownian motion and Itô calculus: filtered information, square-integrable stochastic integrals, localized C1,2 Itô formula, product rule, geometric Brownian motion and its moments. The finite replication argument in options and binomial replication supplies the economic logic. No general change-of-measure theorem is assumed here.

A dealer quotes a call on a dividend-paying share. One analyst predicts 9% annual price appreciation; another predicts 19%. Must their option prices differ? In the model below they can construct the same funded replication. Their forecasts affect physical probabilities, but do not enter the replication cost. Understanding that distinction is more useful than memorizing a formula: it tells us both why drift disappears and why estimating volatility, dividends, funding and trading feasibility still matters.

Define the market, the payout and the trading class

Fix a finite horizon T. Information is the usual completed, right-continuous filtration generated by a Brownian motion WP; P denotes the physical probability model. The ex-dividend price S and cash-account unit B obey

dSt = μSt dt + σSt dWtP,   Bt = ert,   dDt = qSt dt.

Here D is cumulative cash dividends per share, S0 > 0, σ > 0, q ≥ 0, and μ, r, q, σ are finite constants. We later treat σ = 0 and S = 0 separately. Time is in years; r, μ and q are rates per year, while σ is per square-root year. Prices, strike K > 0 and option values are currency units (CU) per share or per single-share contract. μ is the expected price return rate; the expected total-return rate is μ + q. All rates are continuously compounded parameters. The bank account remains strictly positive when r is negative.

Assume continuous trading, divisible positions, no fees or bid–ask spread, unrestricted shorting with dividend compensation, and borrowing and lending at the same r. Dividends are known proportional cash flows and can immediately finance trades. There is no default, taxation, borrowing limit or extra source of risk. A European call pays g(ST) = (ST − K)+ only at T; a put pays (K − ST)+. The option holder receives no interim stock dividend. These are mathematical trading rights, not observations about every actual market.

We use predictable stock holdings Δ and signed bank value b. A positive b is a deposit, and a negative b is debt; the number of bank units is β = b/B. A self-financing portfolio has marked value V = ΔS + b and receives no external contribution after its initial purchase. Its cash accounting is the integral identity corresponding to

dV = Δ(dS + qS dt) + rb dt,   b = V − ΔS. (1)

This is a funding restriction, not the ordinary derivative of ΔS. When Δ and β are continuous semimartingales, the product rule makes the restriction explicit:

S dΔ + d[Δ,S] + B dβ = qΔS dt.

The right side is dividend cash available to pay for rebalancing. Buying extra stock reduces the bank holding; cross-variation belongs in the identity when holdings vary stochastically. We never delete S dΔ by declaring Δ “locally constant.” Equation (1), defined through trading gains, remains the appropriate definition when holdings are only predictable and integrable. For the smooth vanilla hedge the product identity is valid before maturity after localization.

To rule out strategies whose stochastic integrals cannot be averaged, our pricing argument uses a declared class: under the Q constructed below, EQ∫0Te−2ruσ²Su²Δu² du < ∞, together with (1) and finite initial wealth. Discounted gains are then square-integrable martingales. This sufficient admissibility restriction excludes doubling schemes; it is not a characterization of every legitimate strategy in general finance. Call and put hedges satisfy it because their deltas are bounded on a finite horizon and GBM has finite second moments.

The self-financing replication equation

Suppose v(t,s) is C1,2 for t < T and s > 0. On compact regions inside that domain, the preceding chapter's Itô formula applies to v(t,St):

dv = (vt + μS vs + ½σ²S²vss)dt + σS vsdWP.

For V = v to obey (1), its Brownian coefficient must agree with ΔσS. Since σS > 0, Δ = vs. Equality of drift then requires vt + μS vs + ½σ²S²vss = (μ + q)S vs + r(v − Svs). Cancellation gives

vt + ½σ²s²vss + (r − q)s vs − rv = 0,   v(T,s) = g(s). (2)

The physical drift disappears because the same stock exposure supplies both its drift and its risk. The q term does not disappear: stock dividends fund the hedge, whereas the option pays none. Conversely, if a smooth v solves (2), set Δ = vs and b = v − Svs. Itô's formula gives (1) exactly, so these holdings constitute a self-financing strategy, subject to the stated integrability and terminal-limit conditions. This converse verifies the financing, rather than merely labeling a portfolio “hedged.” A different traded price for the same attainable terminal cash would permit taking the cheaper side and financing it by selling the dearer side under the assumed rights.

Haugh's Black–Scholes notes provide a further reading route for replication and dividend-adjusted formulas. The next sections supply the special measure construction, cash-discounting convention and uniqueness conditions needed for our argument.

Construct Q from normal densities

Define the constant market price of risk λ = (μ + q − r)/σ and, for 0 ≤ t ≤ T,

Zt = exp(−λWtP − ½λ²t),   Q(A) = EP[ZT1A]   for A ∈ FT.

Why is this a probability measure? If X is N(0,h), completing the square in its density gives E[eaX] = ea²h/2. Thus EPZt = 1. Also, independent Brownian increments give EP[Zu | Ft] = Zt for u ≥ t. The finite-horizon definition is therefore consistent at earlier times. ZT is strictly positive and finite P-almost surely, so P and Q assign probability zero to exactly the same events: Q is equivalent to P. Its second moment is eλ²T, not one.

We can prove the new Brownian law without quoting general Girsanov. Take a partition 0 = t0 < ⋯ < tn = T, with hi = ti − ti−1 and xi = WtᵢP − Wtᵢ₋₁P. The P-density is a product of centered normal densities. Multiplying it by ZT gives

∏i exp(−xi²/(2hi) − λxi − ½λ²hi)/√(2πhi)
= ∏i exp(−(xi + λhi)²/(2hi))/√(2πhi).

The product factorization shows independent Q-increments with means −λhi and variances hi. For a partition starting at an intermediate t, the conditional-density calculation uses ZT/Zt; the future P-increments are independent of Ft, so the shifted increments are Q-independent of that information as well. Equivalently, test any bounded Ft-measurable variable and any bounded function of the future increments in the definition of Q; the expectation factors after the same square completion. Cylinder events generate the Brownian filtration, and the usual monotone-class extension carries this independence to its sigma-field. The completion does not change the result because the two measures have the same null sets.

Consequently WtQ = WtP + λt starts at zero, has continuous paths and independent centered normal increments of variance equal to elapsed time. It is a Q-Brownian motion. The stock path and its quadratic variation have not changed; its probability weighting has. Substitute WP = WQ − λt into the explicit GBM solution, then apply Itô under Q, to obtain

dS = (r − q)S dt + σS dWQ,   ST = Stexp[(r − q − ½σ²)τ + σ√τ X],   X ∼ N(0,1),   τ = T − t.

This proof covers a finite horizon and constant λ. A stochastic risk premium needs further hypotheses and a genuine general change-of-measure theorem; merely writing an exponential does not make it a martingale. Haugh's stochastic-calculus notes, Sections 12–13, discuss that broader route. We do not infer a theorem for all unbounded strategies, all filtrations or all claims from this elementary construction.

Discount the gains at their actual receipt dates

Under Q, e−rtSt has drift −qe−rtSt and is generally not a martingale. The relevant one-share discounted gain process is

Mt = e−rtSt + ∫0te−ruqSudu,   dMt = e−rtσStdWtQ.

The stochastic coefficient is square-integrable on [0,T], so M is a true martingale. Discounting the sum of uninvested past cash dividends at the final date would be a different expression. Alternatively, reinvest every dividend in stock: the number of shares grows at rate q, total-return wealth Yt = eqtSt, and e−rtYt is also a Q-martingale. One representation discounts each receipt; the other specifies its reinvestment.

Substitution into (1) gives d(e−rtVt) = e−rtΔtσStdWtQ. Within our square-integrable class, conditional expectation therefore implies

v(t,St) = e−rτEQ[g(ST) | Ft]. (3)

A self-financing zero-cost strategy in this class cannot have a nonnegative terminal payoff with positive probability of strict gain: its discounted terminal expectation is zero, while such a payoff would have positive expectation. This proves the relevant no-arbitrage implication directly. Existence of the formula alone does not prove replication for arbitrary claims. For these vanilla claims we will explicitly verify the PDE and construct their admissible deltas. We need neither the general fundamental theorem of asset pricing nor the martingale-representation theorem to prove their prices.

Q is a pricing law under the chosen bank numeraire. It need not be an investor's belief, and risk neutrality is not an assertion about preferences. Under P, E[ST|St=s] = seμτ; under Q it is se(r−q)τ. Both describe the same possible paths with different weights.

Integrate the payoff: why there are two normal terms

Write φ(z) = e−z²/2/√(2π), Φ(x) = ∫−∞xφ(z)dz, and a = σ√τ. For τ > 0 define

d2 = [log(s/K) + (r − q − ½σ²)τ]/a,   d1 = d2 + a.

The call is exercised when X > −d2, so Q(ST > K | St = s) = Φ(d2). The stock-weighted part of the expectation uses the identity eazφ(z) = ea²/2φ(z − a). Therefore

EQ[ST1{ST>K}] = se(r−q−σ²/2)τ∫−d₂∞eazφ(z)dz
= se(r−q)τΦ(d1).

Discount that term and subtract the discounted strike paid on exercise. Integrating below the threshold instead gives E[ST1{ST<K}] = se(r−q)τΦ(−d1) and Q(ST < K) = Φ(−d2). Thus

C(t,s) = se−qτΦ(d1) − Ke−rτΦ(d2),
P(t,s) = Ke−rτΦ(−d2) − se−qτΦ(−d1). (4)

Subtracting gives put–call parity C − P = se−qτ − Ke−rτ. Buying e−qτ shares and reinvesting dividends delivers one share at T; it explains the prepaid-stock term. Φ(d1) is a stock-weighted normal integral, not the Q exercise probability. The call delta will be e−qτΦ(d1), which is neither that probability nor generally Φ(d1) itself.

Verify the PDE, terminal value and uniqueness

Let A = se−qτ and H = Ke−rτ. From d1 − d2 = a one obtains d1² − d2² = 2 log(A/H), hence Aφ(d1) = Hφ(d2). Differentiating (4), the derivatives of the two normal functions cancel in Cs. A second derivative and a calendar-time derivative yield

Cs = e−qτΦ(d1),   Css = e−qτφ(d1)/(sσ√τ),
Ct = −Aφ(d1)σ/(2√τ) + qAΦ(d1) − rHΦ(d2).

In (2), ½σ²s²Css cancels the first term of Ct; the q terms cancel against (r − q)sCs; the remaining r terms cancel against −rC. Parity gives Ps = Cs − e−qτ, Pss = Css and Pt = Ct − qA + rH, verifying the put equation as well. These derivatives hold in the interior. Their bounded deltas and the GBM second moment verify our integrability condition, so the funded portfolios replicate up to T by the terminal limit.

For fixed s, the lognormal St+τ converges in mean square to s as τ ↓ 0. Call and put payoffs are 1-Lipschitz, so their expected payoffs converge to g(s); discounting tends to one. This verifies the terminal condition, including s = K where the payoff has a kink. We require continuity there, not a nonexistent terminal second derivative.

For each fixed positive τ, the spatial boundaries are C(t,0) = 0 and P(t,0) = H. As s → ∞, P → 0 and C − (A − H) → 0. Indeed, 0 ≤ P ≤ H·Q(ST < K), whose probability tends to zero; parity gives the call asymptote. The asymptote is a discounted forward payoff, not the unqualified statement “C tends to S.” Jensen's inequality and payoff domination give

max(A − H,0) ≤ C ≤ A,   max(H − A,0) ≤ P ≤ H.

Uniqueness in a specified class. Consider any v continuous on [0,T] × [0,∞), C1,2 on t < T, s > 0, satisfying (2), the stated terminal payoff, and a uniform linear-growth bound |v(t,s)| ≤ L(1+s) for a finite L. Start at an arbitrary t < T, s > 0 under Q. Stop at ηn, the earlier of T − 1/n and first exit of S from [1/n,n], taking n large enough that t < T − 1/n and s lies inside the interval. Itô applied to e−r(u−t)v(u,Su) has zero drift up to ηn. Its stopped stochastic coefficient is bounded on the relevant compact set, so

v(t,s) = EQ[e−r(ηₙ−t)v(ηn,Sηₙ)].

Positive continuous GBM on a compact horizon has a positive pathwise minimum and finite maximum, so ηn → T almost surely. To pass the expectation through this limit we need more than the word “local.” Write Su = se(r−q)(u−t)Nu, where N is the exponential Brownian martingale. Its second moment is eσ²(u−t); the Doob L² inequality from Chapter 7 bounds E[supt≤u≤TSu²] by 4s²e2|r−q|τ+σ²τ. Hence e|r|τL(1 + sup S) is an integrable dominating random variable. Continuity at T and dominated convergence give (3). Every solution in this class is therefore equal to (4). The boundary at zero is supplied by continuity, since positive GBM never hits zero. This proves uniqueness for our class; it does not assert uniqueness among arbitrary rapidly growing solutions of a backward parabolic equation.

Worked example 1 — dividend cash changes both the hedge and the forecast comparison

A fictional share costs 92 CU. Set K = 100, τ = 1.5 years, r = 0.04, q = 0.015 and σ = 0.25. Assume physical ex-dividend drift μ = 0.09. The standard-deviation scale is a = 0.306186218; A = 92e−0.0225 = 89.953113822 and H = 100e−0.06 = 94.176453358. Thus d1 = 0.003244402 and d2 = −0.302941816. Formula (4) gives C = 9.214855162 and P = 13.438194699. Their difference −4.223339537 equals A − H.

The call hedge holds 0.490141148 shares worth 45.092985629 and has bank value −35.878130467 CU; the purchase is financed by the option premium and that borrowing. The put hedge holds −0.487610089 shares with a 58.298322892 CU deposit. No dividend is paid directly to either option holder; dividends from the hedge stock enter (1).

The call's Q exercise probability is 0.380967102. Its physical probability is Φ([log(92/100) + (0.09 − 0.25²/2)1.5]/a) = 0.506180107. Neither equals delta. Expected terminal stock is 105.297384160 under P and 95.515503732 under Q. Under Q the discounted ex-price expectation is 89.953113822 and discounted dividend receipts have expectation 92(1 − e−0.0225) = 2.046886178, summing to the current 92. Omitting dividends would destroy that martingale reconciliation.

Worked example 2 — a density changes weights, not the observed stock path

For the same parameters λ = (0.09 + 0.015 − 0.04)/0.25 = 0.26. Consider three half-year Brownian P-increments 0.1, −0.2, 0.3 as a point at which to evaluate densities. Their sum is 0.2. Log ZT = −0.26(0.2) − ½(0.26²)(1.5) = −0.1027, so ZT = 0.902397652. This is a density ratio, not the probability of that exact continuous path, which is zero.

The corresponding WQ increments on this path are 0.23, −0.07, 0.43. Under Q, WTP has mean −0.39 and variance 1.5, whereas WTQ has mean zero and variance 1.5. Multiplying three shifted normal densities gives log joint Q-density −1.959794829; subtracting log joint P-density −1.857094829 gives −0.1027. Independently, EPZT = 1 and EPZT² = e0.1014 = 1.106719241. A single density evaluation illustrates the algebra; normalization and independence were proved above for all increments.

Degenerate inputs, negative rates and dividend contracts

τ = 0. The values are exactly (s − K)+ and (K − s)+. Do not divide by √τ or invoke d1. At the strike the payoff delta is not uniquely defined; away from it one-sided time limits and payoff derivatives must still be distinguished. The laboratory deliberately reports no expiry Greeks.

S = 0. With the multiplicative stock model, zero is absorbing. Dividends then vanish, the call is zero, and the put is certain cash K discounted to Ke−rτ. Derivatives reported by the lab at zero are right-hand limits of the family indexed by initial spot. They are not uniquely determined hedge holdings in an economy whose stock is identically zero. No λ needs to be assigned at this absorbing state.

σ = 0 and S > 0. The physical stock path is deterministic. Reinvested dividends grow total stock wealth at μ + q, so the no-arbitrage model requires μ + q = r. If these rates differ, borrow the lower-growth asset and buy the higher-growth asset under the stated reversible rights; changing probabilities cannot remove a deterministic gain. With equality, ST = se(r−q)τ, and C = (A − H)+, P = (H − A)+. There is no division by σ and no need for a unique Brownian pricing measure. At A = H these prices have a kink as functions of s; delta and gamma are not supplied. This deterministic economy must be distinguished from the σ ↓ 0 limit of positive-volatility models with unconstrained physical drifts.

r < 0. B is positive but decreases. All exponentials, the tilt and the PDE remain valid. H may exceed K, and the European put upper bound is H rather than K. Some familiar comparisons to immediate exercise require additional rate assumptions. The formula here remains European and contains no early-exercise decision.

A scheduled cash dividend is a different model. If a known cash payment D occurs at td, an idealized ex-dividend jump is St_d = St_d− − D wherever the post-payment price is nonnegative. A no-payout European option satisfies the matching condition v(td−,s) = v(td,s − D), with further modeling required if the cash promise exceeds available stock value. Between dates one can solve an appropriate diffusion equation, but the terminal stock is generally not the single lognormal variable used in (4). Subtracting present-valued dividends from spot is a modeling approximation unless the dynamics of the adjusted asset and all cash rights justify it. A continuous proportional yield preserves GBM; a fixed cash jump does not.

Worked example 3 — cases that a single formula call must not conceal

For S = 103, K = 100, τ = 0.75, r = −0.02, q = 0.01 and σ = 0.30, A = 102.230389646 and H = 101.511306462. We obtain C = 10.892518857, P = 10.173435672, and C − P = 0.719083185. Negative r creates no division problem. The right upper bound for this put is 101.511306462.

Now consider a separate deterministic share with S = 90, K = 100, τ = 2, r = −0.01, q = 0.02 and σ = 0. A consistent physical drift is μ = −0.03. Terminal stock is 84.758808023; A = 86.471049524 and H = 102.020134003. The call is zero and the put is 15.549084479. Replacing spot by zero makes the put 102.020134003, exceeding the undiscounted strike. At τ = 0 with S = K = 100 both payoffs are zero. A fourth separate case, S = K = 100, r = q = 0.02, μ = 0 and σ = 0, has A = H and zero prices but no unique spot derivative at its deterministic exercise threshold.

Worked example 4 — self-financing does not make a coarse hedge exact

Start the long call hedge of Worked example 1 with its premium 9.214855162. At half-year dates observe invented ex-prices 92, 97, 88, 110. Between delta resets, reinvest proportional dividends continuously in stock and leave bank units unchanged. If n shares and b CU are held after a reset, the next incoming shares are n eqh, the bank before trading is b erh, and wealth is n eqhS′ + b erh. Reset to the new model delta by paying (Δ′ − n eqh)S′ from the bank. At expiry sell all shares and compare with the call payoff.

At the first reset incoming shares are 0.493831026 and bank is −36.602916780. Buying the extra shares costs 3.802066146, leaving bank −40.404982926. Every external contribution after inception is zero. Nevertheless the terminal hedge exceeds the payoff by 2.143362474 CU; a different sequence can produce a deficit. This is a deterministic cash illustration, not a sampled estimate of expected profit. Continuous dividend reinvestment between dates does not implement continuous delta adjustment. The table anticipates the hedge-error analysis of Greeks, volatility and hedging.

Reproducible lab and an honest model-use boundary

The original lab provides eight input cases, a standard-library Python model, full output, a four-file SHA256 manifest and standalone instructions. Run python3 v10-c08-analysis.py --input v10-c08-inputs.json --output result.json; the same command works with python3 -O. Import and run(data) are quiet and do not mutate inputs. The specified bounded domain rejects malformed keys, booleans, nonfinite values and inconsistent deterministic drift, and reports unavailable derivatives as JSON null.

The package preserves the three original interior/boundary price examples and the expiry and absorbing cases, adding a symmetric zero-carry price, a deterministic threshold and a far-tail numerical stress. Prices use the out-of-the-money expression plus parity to reduce cancellation; extremely small tails can underflow to zero, so the checker uses an absolute currency tolerance rather than promising relative accuracy for every tiny option. An unrepresentably small density ratio is explicitly null with an underflow flag while its finite log is retained; it is never interpreted as a zero-probability event. Independent quadrature of terminal-payoff integrals, finite-difference sensitivities, exact density factorization and reconstructed financing provide separate checks. None makes a numerical illustration a proof of a continuous-time theorem.

In a research or risk application, identify the deliverable and expiry convention, ex-dividend cash model, units, funding assumptions and input timestamp before calibration. An implied volatility is the σ that matches one option quotation in the chosen formula; fitting that quotation is an algebraic inversion. It does not prove constant physical volatility, lognormal tails or perfect executable hedging. Different inferred volatilities across strikes challenge the one-σ specification under otherwise identical assumptions; changes in dividends, dates, quotes and contract rights must also be checked before drawing that conclusion. The next chapters examine these sensitivities and computational errors. No present-day market data are used here.

Exercises

Problems use the idealized market above unless a changed assumption is explicit. Use the full formulas or the downloadable lab for numerical values, retain at least six decimals in intermediate work, and report currency answers to six decimals. Exercises 2, 3, 4 and 7 require arguments, not just numerical checks.

  1. Ex-price versus total gain

    In Worked example 1 compute EQ[e−rTST] and EQ∫0Te−ruqSudu. Derive the expressions for general s and T starting at zero, including q = 0. Explain why e−rtSt alone is not the martingale when q > 0, and distinguish μ from μ + q.

  2. Derive a funded PDE

    Starting from V = ΔS + βB, state the self-financing gains equation with dividend cash, derive the product-rule rebalancing identity, then use Itô to derive (2). Give the converse construction of Δ and bank value from a smooth solution and the integrability condition used to price it. Identify the error in differentiating v − ΔS while dropping S dΔ and d[Δ,S].

  3. Prove the constant tilt

    For λ = 0.26 prove normalization and the martingale property of Z. Complete the square for an interval h = 0.25 and identify the mean and variance of the P-Brownian increment under Q. Explain why omitting the correction −½λ²t would break normalization, prove independence for a finite partition and identify WQ. State what this proof does not establish for stochastic λ.

  4. Derive, then simplify, the payoff integrals

    Derive both expressions in (4) from the upper and lower truncated lognormal integrals. For s = K = 100, r = q = 0, σ = 0.20 and τ = 1, compute C, P, delta and Q exercise probability. Explain why delta exceeds the exercise probability in this particular case. Is that inequality a general dividend-adjusted identity?

  5. Change a forecast while holding tradable inputs fixed

    Change μ in Worked example 1 from 0.09 to 0.19. Compute λ and the physical exercise probability. Which of C, P, delta, Q exercise probability and the cash needed to initiate the hedge changes? Explain why “the model ignores expected returns” is an incomplete description.

  6. Audit the derivatives and PDE

    Prove Aφ(d1) = Hφ(d2) and use it to derive Cs. For Worked example 1 compute Css, Ct, Ps and Pt, and substitute into both pricing equations. Specify whether your time derivative holds T or τ fixed. Explain the limitation of a near-zero numerical residual.

  7. Prove uniqueness in the declared class

    Suppose v and w are continuous through T, C1,2 in the interior, obey the same PDE and terminal payoff, and each satisfies a uniform linear-growth bound. Prove v = w by the stopped stochastic-integral argument. Identify why the stopping integral has zero expectation, why the stopping times approach T and what permits the limit inside expectation. Would the words “local martingale” alone suffice?

  8. Zero volatility is an economic restriction

    Recompute the deterministic call and put in Worked example 3. Now change only μ to zero, keeping σ = 0. Construct a zero-cost arbitrage using the stock with reinvested dividends and the bank, and compute its certain terminal profit over two years. Explain why an equivalent probability change cannot repair this input. For the separate deterministic threshold case in that example, discuss delta.

  9. Boundary conditions with negative interest

    For S = 0, K = 100, r = −0.01 and τ = 2, price both options and explain why the put can exceed K. State the correct large-s call asymptote at q > 0, and the τ = 0 value at s = K. Using the expectation representation, justify both call bounds and both put bounds without assuming r ≥ 0.

  10. Replace a yield by a cash dividend

    A share goes from 100 immediately before a known 4 CU cash dividend to 96 immediately after it, with no other price move. State the matching condition for a European no-payout option and reconcile the stock-holder's total cash gain across the date. For a separate time-zero share price 100, r = 0, T = 1 and that single payment before T, find the continuous yield q whose prepaid-delivery value matches 100 − 4. Does the match prove equal option prices? Address the nonnegative-stock boundary.

  11. Rebalance with no new cash

    Reconstruct the first half-year row of Worked example 4 from inception holdings. At year 1 keep its shares and bank unchanged, but replace the final observed stock price 110 by 40. Reinvest dividends, accrue the bank, liquidate the shares and compute the final call payoff and hedge error. Explain why the first positive error and this negative error neither prove an arbitrage nor validate continuous replication.

  12. Referee a model-validation claim

    A memo says: “We fit each strike's implied volatility, so the stock has constant physical volatility. We use call delta as exercise probability and replace every cash dividend by an equivalent yield, exactly. The discounted ex-price must be a martingale. A coarse hedge made money on our selected path, so replication is exact and funding risk is absent.” Write a correction addressing every claim. Propose a reproducible validation protocol that distinguishes formula implementation, input/contract errors and empirical adequacy. Explain the limited role of the chapter's primary readings and give at least two numerical or analytical counterexamples from this chapter.

Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. Discount each dividend when received

    EQSu = se(r−q)u, so the ex-price expectation is se−qT. By nonnegativity (or absolute integrability), expectation can pass through the dividend integral, giving ∫0Tqse−qudu = s(1 − e−qT). For q = 0 the integral is zero and the first term equals s, without dividing by q. The example gives 89.953113822 and 2.046886178, summing to 92. Itô gives drift −qe−rtSt for the discounted ex-price; adding discounted dividends cancels it. μ = 0.09 describes physical price appreciation and μ + q = 0.105 the instantaneous expected total return. Neither is the Q ex-price drift r − q = 0.025.

  2. The bank pays for changes in holdings

    Self-financing means dV = ΔdS + qΔSdt + βdB. Product differentiation of ΔS + βB gives ΔdS + S dΔ + d[Δ,S] + βdB + B dβ, since B has finite variation. Equating the two expressions proves S dΔ + d[Δ,S] + B dβ = qΔSdt. Itô gives diffusion σS vs, while gains give ΔσS. With σS > 0, Δ = vs and βB = v − Svs. Equating drifts leaves vt + ½σ²S²vss + (r − q)Svs − rv = 0.

    Conversely choose those Δ and β for an interior smooth PDE solution. Itô then agrees with the gains identity, which proves funding before maturity; terminal continuity gives the payoff. We additionally require EQ∫e−2ruσ²S²Δ²du < ∞ to take conditional expectations of discounted gains. This is checked for the call and put using bounded delta and GBM moments. Dropping the holding-change and cross-variation terms from a product derivative falsely assumes the rebalancing cash disappears. In the valid argument the bank explicitly offsets them after dividend receipts.

  3. Normalization, independence and the sign of the drift

    The normal exponential moment gives E e−λWₜ = eλ²t/2, canceled by e−λ²t/2. Writing Zu = Zt exp[−λ(Wu − Wt) − ½λ²(u − t)] and conditioning proves E[Zu|Ft] = Zt. Without the correction the expectation is eλ²t/2, not one (unless λ = 0 or t = 0).

    For h = 0.25 the exponent −x²/(2h) − 0.26x − ½(0.26²)h equals −(x + 0.26h)²/(2h). Thus the increment has Q-mean −0.065 and variance 0.25. For several intervals, Z factors into the corresponding interval factors and the P-density factors into independent normals, so their product factors into shifted normal densities. Conditional on earlier information the same factorization uses ZT/Zt. WQ = WP + 0.26t has centered independent normal increments and continuous paths. Strict positivity of Z makes the measures equivalent on the finite horizon. With stochastic λ, this simple density factorization is unavailable; proving normalization, conditional laws and the relevant integrability requires additional results. No conclusion is justified by merely substituting a random process into this proof.

  4. A stock-weighted expectation and an event probability

    The call's exercise threshold is X > −d2. The probability integral is Φ(d2); square completion in its stock term gives se(r−q)τΦ(d2 + a). Below the threshold the corresponding integrals are Φ(−d2) and se(r−q)τΦ(−d2 − a). Discount and subtract the respective strike/stock terms to obtain both formulas. At zero carry with s = K, d1 = 0.1 and d2 = −0.1, so C = P = 100[2Φ(0.1) − 1] = 7.965567455 CU. Delta is 0.539827837 and Q exercise probability is 0.460172163.

    Here q = 0 and d1 > d2, so the increasing CDF proves the stated ordering. In the general formula delta includes e−qτ. A sufficiently large yield and sufficiently deep in-the-money option can have delta below its exercise probability. The general identities are Δ = e−qτΦ(d1) and Q(exercise) = Φ(d2), not a universal ordering.

  5. Physical risk still changes

    λ = (0.19 + 0.015 − 0.04)/0.25 = 0.66. The physical exercise probability becomes Φ([log(0.92) + (0.19 − 0.03125)1.5]/0.306186218) = 0.693357459, up from 0.506180107. C, P, delta, Q exercise probability and initial hedge cash all remain the Worked example 1 values. The density relating P to Q changes precisely so that the Q ex-price drift remains r − q. Forecasts still matter for physical risk, expected investment outcomes and empirical testing. Their absence from this attainable claim's replication cost does not eliminate their role in those different questions.

  6. Analytical cancellation before numerical residuals

    Let ℓ = log(A/H). Then d1 = (ℓ + a²/2)/a and d2 = (ℓ − a²/2)/a; their squared difference is 2ℓ. Consequently φ(d1)/φ(d2) = e−ℓ = H/A. Since ∂d1/∂s = ∂d2/∂s = 1/(sa), the normal-density derivative terms in Cs cancel, leaving e−qτΦ(d1).

    The example gives Css = 0.013847223, Ct = −4.421320938, Ps = −0.487610089 and Pt = −2.003559511. Gamma is the same for the put. Substituting into Ct + 0.025(92)Cs + ½(0.25²)(92²)Css − 0.04C yields zero analytically; the put substitution does too. Full-precision lab residuals are at floating roundoff. Time derivatives hold maturity T fixed, so ∂/∂t = −∂/∂τ. A residual at one parameter set cannot verify the PDE everywhere, establish boundary values, prove uniqueness or validate market assumptions; it may also share a coding error with the derivatives.

  7. Growth supplies the missing limit argument

    Set u = v − w. It obeys the homogeneous PDE, terminal value zero and a uniform bound |u| ≤ L′(1+s). Stop inside [1/n,n] and before T − 1/n. The discounted stopped u has zero drift; derivatives and stock are bounded on that compact time/space set, so its Brownian coefficient is square-integrable. The Itô integral has expectation zero, hence u(t,s) = E[e−r(ηₙ−t)u(ηn,Sηₙ)] without assuming an unstopped martingale theorem.

    Strict positivity and continuity of GBM imply a positive minimum and finite maximum on each full finite path, so eventually no spatial exit occurs and ηn → T. The exponential-martingale representation and Doob's inequality give a finite second moment for sup S, hence a finite first moment. The growth bound supplies domination by e|r|τL′(1 + sup S). Continuity through T and dominated convergence send the right side to zero. Thus u(t,s) = 0 for all interior points, and continuity extends equality to the boundary. “Local martingale” alone does not justify taking an unstopped expectation or exchanging this limit. The proof uses an explicit dominating integrable variable.

  8. A deterministic return gap cannot be reweighted away

    With the consistent μ = −0.03, the terminal price is 90e−0.06 = 84.758808023. The call is 0, and the put is 100e0.02 − 90e−0.04 = 15.549084479 CU. With the changed μ = 0, buy one share for 90 using 90 borrowed from the bank, and reinvest its dividends. At T = 2, its total wealth is 90e0.04; debt is 90e−0.02. The initial cost is zero and the certain net profit is 90(e0.04 − e−0.02) = 5.455089080 CU. All cash terms follow the symmetric borrowing/shorting assumptions.

    An equivalent probability measure preserves sure events, so it cannot change that deterministic inequality. In the separate threshold case A = H, the call is max(A − H,0); its left spot derivative is zero and its right derivative is e−qτ. The put has left derivative −e−qτ and right derivative zero. No unique derivative exists at the kink, though the zero terminal cash in that exact economy can simply be replicated by holding zero. Reporting a universal delta there would conflate a price sensitivity with one possible replication.

  9. Bounds are discounted, not tied to the sign of r

    At zero spot the call is 0 and the put is 100e0.02 = 102.020134003 CU. Buying that much cash today leaves exactly 100 at maturity in a negative-rate bank. The large-s asymptote is C − [se−qτ − Ke−rτ] → 0. At τ = 0 and s = K both payoffs are zero; the payoff kink has no unique delta.

    Nonnegativity gives each lower bound zero. Jensen gives E[(ST − K)+] ≥ (E ST − K)+ and the analogous put inequality; multiplying by the positive discount factor gives lower bounds (A − H)+ and (H − A)+. Pointwise (ST − K)+ ≤ ST and (K − ST)+ ≤ K give upper bounds A and H. Every argument needs positive discounting, which holds for all finite r; none requires e−rτ ≤ 1.

  10. The jump must preserve total cash

    The matching condition is v(td−,100) = v(td,96). One share loses 4 of marked ex-price and receives 4 of cash, for zero total jump gain; Δ shares lose 4Δ and receive 4Δ. A no-payout option holder does not receive that 4 directly. Under the separate r = 0 forward-carry calculation, 100e−q = 96 gives q = −log(0.96) = 0.040821995 per year.

    Matching this one prepaid-delivery value matches a first-moment/carry condition under those rights. It does not match the distribution of stock or the timing of cash and exercise. A fixed cash jump generally destroys the single-GBM terminal distribution, so it does not prove equal convex option expectations. If a stock just before the payment can be below 4, the unconditional rule S′ = S − 4 would produce a negative value; an additional rule for payment reduction, default, financing or a different asset model is required. Ignoring that boundary is not an exact extension of our positive-stock model.

  11. A cash ledger can produce either sign of error

    At year 0.5, incoming shares are 0.490141148e0.0075 = 0.493831026 and bank is −35.878130467e0.02 = −36.602916780. Wealth is 97(0.493831026) − 36.602916780 = 11.298692790. The new delta is 0.533027585, so purchase cost is 3.802066146, leaving bank −40.404982926. Wealth is unchanged by this funded trade.

    For the changed last interval, incoming shares are 0.284225207e0.0075 = 0.286364910, and bank before liquidation is −18.973487712e0.02 = −19.356777589. Selling the shares for 40 each leaves −7.902181202 CU. The call payoff is zero, so this is also the hedge error: additional cash would be needed to discharge the hedge's debt. Up to that debt settlement the ledger has no external contributions; self-financing does not mean solvent on every coarse path. The positive result on the original sequence and this loss on another refute any path-independent profit claim. They also use discrete delta resets, whereas the theorem's strategy adjusts delta continuously under its stipulated stochastic model.

  12. Correct the inference, then test each layer

    Fitting a separate σ at each strike is a quote representation; differing fitted values contradict a single constant σ under a common correct contract specification and accurate contemporaneous inputs. It does not estimate constant physical volatility. Exercise probability under Q is Φ(d2), while delta is e−qτΦ(d1); neither is automatically a physical probability. A carry-equivalent yield does not reproduce a fixed-dividend jump distribution. Discounted total gains, including correctly dated dividend cash, form the martingale; the ex-price alone has drift −q times its discounted value. A selected coarse hedge can profit or lose and requires financing even when no external cash is contributed during rebalancing. Borrowing limits or a different funding rate would alter the exercise's implementation assumptions.

    Concrete counterexamples include delta 0.490141148 versus Q probability 0.380967102 and physical probability 0.506180107 in Worked example 1; the omitted discounted dividend cash 2.046886178; and coarse terminal errors +2.143362474 and −7.902181202. The cash-dividend exercise shows identical prepaid value without an identical stochastic process. Two correctly explained counterexamples suffice; more digits alone earn no credit.

    A reproducible protocol freezes contract rights, price timestamps, bid/ask quotes, expiry clock, units, discount and dividend assumptions, then checks parity and model bounds. Test the implementation against independently integrated payoff expectations, analytical boundaries, finite differences and a cash-ledger reconstruction; preserve inputs, code, tolerances and hashes. For empirical adequacy, define before evaluation an out-of-sample option/hedging sample, matched contracts, dividend events, executable spread and funding costs, rebalance schedule, risk metric and exclusions. Compare residual distributions across maturity, moneyness and event days, checking input errors before attributing them to stochastic-volatility or jump mechanisms. A fit within the same sample and selected successful paths are inadequate tests.

    Evaluation. Full credit requires correction of all six claims (volatility inference, probability, dividends, discounted gains, exact coarse replication and absent funding risk), two correct counterexamples, separate implementation and empirical tests, reproducible evidence, and honest source scope. The cited teaching notes support mathematical methods and a route to broader theory; they do not authenticate current quotes, executed trading rights or the synthetic paths, and they do not provide empirical validation of this lab. Alternative test designs are acceptable when they identify their target and possible confounders. Neither a successful test nor this author review guarantees future hedging performance.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain to a learner why a dividend-paying stock has Q ex-price drift r − q, why delta is not exercise probability, and how continuous trading enters the pricing claim.

Model answer. The bank is the pricing numeraire. Under Q, its discount factor makes total stock gains a martingale. Dividends supply qSdt, so the remaining ex-price drift is (r − q)Sdt. A call pays stock minus strike only above a threshold: its stock-weighted integral and its event-probability integral have different normal arguments. Delta is e−qτΦ(d1), while Q exercise probability is Φ(d2). A funded strategy holds delta shares and finances the residual bank value, continuously adjusting as t and S change. That strategy, with stated admissibility and terminal conditions, explains the unique model price. A finite trading schedule leaves a random hedge error and must be evaluated separately.

Delayed retention, after 7–14 days. Without looking up the formula: (i) derive the sign of q in the pricing PDE from cash flows; (ii) with s = K = 100, r = q = 0, σ = 0.2 and τ = 1, express the call price using Φ(0.1); (iii) give the zero-spot put price for K = 50, r = −0.02 and τ = 1; (iv) for μ = 0.08, q = 0.02, r = 0.04, σ = 0.30, give λ and WQ; (v) state the terminal regularity and growth conditions used in the uniqueness proof.

Answers. (i) The stock hedge earns qΔSdt and the option does not; equating drift yields (r − q)svs in the PDE. (ii) C = 100[2Φ(0.1) − 1] = 7.965567455. (iii) P = 50e0.02 = 51.010067001 CU. (iv) λ = 0.20 and WtQ = WtP + 0.20t on the fixed horizon, under the measure with density exp(−0.20WTP − 0.02T). (v) Continuity through T with the prescribed payoff, interior C1,2 regularity and a uniform bound L(1+s), combined with the GBM supremum moment, justify the stopped expectation limit. Advancement requires all five explanations and a fresh funded hedge ledger whose final error is not presumed zero.

Sources and further development

Martin Haugh, The Black–Scholes Model (2016), Sections 1–3, supplies a primary course treatment of replication, continuous yields and sensitivity interpretation. Haugh, Introduction to Stochastic Calculus for Diffusions (2013), Sections 12–13, supplies further study on measure changes and trading gains; its general theorems require the additional technical conditions identified there. The chapter's finite-horizon normal-density proof, explicit uniqueness class, original cases and exercises stand on their stated assumptions. Vasily Strela's MIT lecture on Black–Scholes and risk-neutral valuation (Fall 2013), transcript pages 7–12, is an alternative exposition of replication, boundaries and the distinction between formula use and a common volatility specification.

These are historical mathematical teaching sources, not current contract specifications. We do not adopt informal unqualified martingale statements or infer physical calibration from them. General stochastic risk premiums, arbitrary-claim completeness, jumps, transaction costs, stochastic volatility and the analysis of American exercise require further theory. The next chapter develops sensitivities and hedge risk within and beyond the present constant-coefficient benchmark.

Sources and further study

  • Martin Haugh — The Black–Scholes Model (2016) — Further reading on stock/cash replication, constant continuous dividend yield, call/put formulas and the distinction between delta and risk-neutral exercise probability. Original chapter proofs, numbers and problems are independently developed.
  • Martin Haugh — Introduction to Stochastic Calculus for Diffusions (Fall 2013) — Further study on constant exponential-normal tilts, the additional hypotheses for general Girsanov, self-financing product terms and continuously reinvested dividends. This chapter proves only its finite-horizon constant-coefficient case and vanilla pricing uniqueness.
  • Vasily Strela / MIT OpenCourseWare — Lecture 19: Black–Scholes Formula, Risk-neutral Valuation, 18.S096 (Fall 2013 transcript) — Alternative primary teaching exposition of the replication-to-PDE route, terminal/boundary data and the distinction between a common volatility model and strike-specific implied volatilities.
